items.body:
The e2e test framework has several patterns that cause flakiness, silent resource leaks, and hard-to-debug failures, especially in disruptive tests that restart API servers or control plane components. PR 137832 addresses these across 13 files (185 additions, 41 deletions), touching SIG api-machinery, apps, cloud-provider, network, node, storage, and testing.

Error suppression hides resource leaks. Across the test suite, cleanup code discards errors from Delete calls. In test/e2e/apimachinery/aggregator.go, the cleanupSampleAPIServer function has 10 such calls (APIService, Deployment, Secret, Service, ServiceAccount, RoleBinding, ClusterRoleBinding, ClusterRole) all silently swallowed. Same pattern in test/e2e/apimachinery/apply.go (4 deployments/pods), test/e2e/apps/rc.go (DeleteCollection), and test/e2e/apps/statefulset.go (ConfigMaps in defer blocks). When these fail, resources leak into subsequent tests with zero trace of what went wrong.

No retry on transient API server errors. GetControlPlaneNodes in test/e2e/framework/util.go calls Nodes().List() and immediately fails on any error. During disruptive tests (daemon restarts, etcd failure injection), the API server is expected to be briefly unreachable. The same issue exists in allNodesReady at test/e2e/framework/node/helper.go and RestartNodes at test/e2e/common/util.go. A transient connection refused or 503 kills the entire test instead of retrying. The fix introduces IsRetryableAPIError which checks for connection refused/reset, server timeout, 429, 503, 500, and unexpected server errors, plus a new WaitForControlPlaneNodes that wraps the listing in a polling loop with retry-on-transient logic.

Healthz returns 200 before daemon is ready. RestartDaemonConfig.waitUp in test/e2e/apps/daemon_restart.go considers the daemon ready when /healthz returns HTTP 200. After a kubelet restart, the health endpoint can report ok while kubelet is still recovering. Logs show errors, pods are not yet scheduled. The fix adds verifyDaemonReadiness which SSHes into the node and checks the last 20 lines of /var/log/kubelet.log for error patterns before declaring readiness.

Goroutines not gracefully stopped. In test/e2e/apps/daemon_restart.go, a cache.NewInformer controller is started with go controller.Run(backgroundCtx.Done()). The cleanup calls cancel() but does not wait for the controller goroutine to finish. The fix replaces this with a dedicated stopCh channel and DeferCleanup that closes the channel then sleeps 100ms to allow graceful shutdown.

PVC deletion races with pod references. DeleteAllStatefulSets in test/e2e/framework/statefulset/rest.go has a TODO comment about not checking whether pods still reference PVCs before deleting them. The current code deletes PVCs immediately, which can fail or leave orphaned PVs when pods are still running. The fix lists pods, checks volume references, and only deletes PVCs that are not in use, with foreground propagation.

Duplicated control plane filtering. GetControlPlaneNodes and WaitForControlPlaneNodes both contain the same node filtering logic (check for control-plane label and NoSchedule taint). The second commit extracts this into a shared filterControlPlaneNodes helper.

All changes are in e2e test code, no user-facing impact.

Related issues:
- 109600: prevent the Expect(err).NotTo(HaveOccurred()) and ExpectNoError(err) anti-pattern in e2e tests (same category of error handling problems)
- 86253: sample-apiserver returns error instead of falling back to second Accept type (directly affects the aggregator.go test modified in this PR)
- 135285: GOAWAY are not handled gracefully in apiserver when aggregating (related network error handling)
- 105536: Orphaned pod found, but error not a directory occurred when trying to remove the volumes dir (related resource cleanup issue)

https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/pull/37410 points out that the single `[Feature:Networking-IPv6]` e2e test and the `[Feature:SCTPConnectivity]` tests do not get run by any of our existing CI jobs.

`[Feature:Networking-IPv6]` requires connectivity to the IPv6 internet, which our default CI environment doesn't have.
`[Feature:SCTPConnectivity]` requires kernel support for SCTP (which the default GCE "COS" kernels don't have) and pod network support for SCTP (which, AIUI, the GCE underlay network does not have, so these tests can't run in an environment that sends pod network packets directly over the GCE underlay). Also, some of the SCTP tests are also `[Feature:NetworkPolicy]`, so we should run it in an environment with NP. And one of the SCTP tests is `[Feature:IPv6DualStack]`.

@upodroid [points out](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/pull/37410#issuecomment-4941003690) that the `k8s-infra-aks-prow-build` cluster supports dual-stack and has external IPv6 connectivity. It seems that the `eks-prow-build-cluster` also supports dual-stack clusters, though I'm not sure if it supports dual-stack external connectivity.

I'm not sure about the state of SCTP support in the default kernels on those platforms, or if we have infra for running non-default-kernels on jobs on those platforms...

Anyway, we should add a periodic that runs on EKS or AKS with a config that allows for `[Feature:IPv6DualStack]`, `[Feature:Networking-IPv6]`, `[Feature:SCTPConnectivity]`, and `[Feature:NetworkPolicy]`.

items.title: kube-proxy: stale UDP conntrack entries are never cleaned up when a service scales down to zero endpoints

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/network
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Network.

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR is ready to be actively worked on.

items.body:
### What happened?

When a UDP service with active senders is scaled down to zero endpoints, the conntrack entries established while the endpoints existed are never removed. The conntrack reconciler introduced in v1.32 (#127318) skips services without serving endpoints:

```go
// pkg/proxy/conntrack/cleanup.go
// a Service without endpoints does not require to clean the conntrack entries associated.
if endpoints.Len() == 0 {
    continue
}
```

The `REJECT` rule installed for a service with no endpoints does not help for those pre-existing flows: packets are DNATed to the (deleted) endpoint IP by conntrack before the filter rule, which matches on the service ClusterIP, can be evaluated. For one-way UDP traffic (statsd/dogstatsd-style, conntrack entries permanently `[UNREPLIED]`), every packet refreshes the 30s `nf_conntrack_udp_timeout`, so the stale entries and the blackholed traffic persist indefinitely.

In our production case (statsd at ~64k pkt/s cluster-wide), all senders kept DNAT-ing to the deleted pod IP for 13 hours. All that traffic converges on the node that owns the deleted pod IP's CIDR block and is dropped there in `NET_RX`, which held a single 8-core node at ~60-73% softirq for the whole duration. Recovery is instant once the service gets an endpoint again, because the reconciler then processes the service and deletes every entry whose reply-source is not the new endpoint.

Observed evidence on v1.33.5 (iptables mode, controlled reproduction, ~3.5 min after scaling to 0, kube-proxy already synced):

```
# REJECT rule is installed:
-A KUBE-SERVICES -d 10.0.200.123/32 -p udp -m comment --comment "test/udp-sink:statsd has no endpoints" -j REJECT --reject-with icmp-port-unreachable

# yet the stale entry persists and keeps refreshing (pod 10.244.5.127 deleted minutes ago):
udp 17 29 src=10.244.9.181 dst=10.0.200.123 sport=12345 dport=9125 [UNREPLIED] src=10.244.5.127 dst=10.244.9.181 sport=9125 dport=12345

# reconciler ran but deleted nothing:
kubeproxy_conntrack_reconciler_deleted_entries_total{ip_family="IPv4"} 1151   # unchanged

# after scaling back to 1 replica: counter 1151 -> 1152, entry deleted, traffic restored instantly
```

This is a regression versus <=1.31: the event-based cleanup (`DeletedUDPEndpoints` in the pre-reconciler `CleanStaleEntries`) cleared entries for every deleted UDP endpoint regardless of how many endpoints remained, so the N->0 transition was covered.

### What did you expect to happen?

Scaling a UDP service to zero endpoints removes the conntrack entries DNAT-ing to the deleted endpoints, the same way scaling from N to M>0 does. New packets then hit the `REJECT` rule (which also prevents new conntrack entries from being confirmed), and senders receive ICMP port-unreachable instead of blackholing traffic to a deleted pod IP forever.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a UDP deployment + ClusterIP service (port 9125), 1 replica.
2. From a pod on a different node, send UDP to the ClusterIP from a single long-lived socket (fixed source port) at any steady rate, e.g. 5 pkt/s:
   `while true; do echo ping; sleep 0.2; done | nc -u -p 12345 <ClusterIP> 9125`
3. `kubectl scale deploy/<name> --replicas=0` and wait for the pod to be deleted.
4. On the sender's node, run `conntrack -L -p udp --orig-port-dst 9125`. The entry persists indefinitely (timeout refreshed by every packet), DNAT-ing to the deleted pod IP, even though `iptables-save | grep "has no endpoints"` shows the REJECT rule. `kubeproxy_conntrack_reconciler_deleted_entries_total` does not increase.
5. `kubectl scale --replicas=1`: the entry is deleted on the next sync (counter increments), confirming the reconciler handles the service again as soon as it has an endpoint.

### Anything else we need to know?

- The skip was discussed in the #127318 review: the rationale was that the REJECT rule protects services without endpoints. That holds for new flows (REJECT prevents conntrack confirmation) but not for flows established before the endpoints were removed, which bypass the rule via early DNAT.
- iptables and nftables modes share this code path; both are affected. IPVS is not (`expire_nodest_conn=1`).
- Mitigations we use: never scale one-way UDP services to 0; emergency fix is scaling back to >=1 replica (instant) or `conntrack -D -p udp --orig-port-dst <port>` on sender nodes.
- We have a fix ready and will open a PR shortly.

### Kubernetes version

<details>

Observed on v1.33.5 (AKS, kube-proxy iptables mode). The skip is still present in master (`pkg/proxy/conntrack/cleanup.go`).

</details>

### Cloud provider

<details>

AKS (Azure CNI Overlay), but the issue is provider-independent; reproduced with plain kube-proxy + conntrack.

</details>

/kind bug
/sig network

items.body:
### What happened?

During HNS restart stress scenarios combined with rapid pod scale operations, Windows KubeProxy intermittently fails to recreate LoadBalancers and logs the following error:

``` hcnCreateLoadBalancer failed in Win32: Cannot create a file when that file already exists. (0xb7) ```

While HNS was temporarily unavailable, KubeProxy attempted to reconcile proxy rules. During this window:

- GetHNSNetwork failed because HNS was down.
- KubeProxy proceeded with LoadBalancer cleanup logic.
- GetLoadBalancer calls also failed due to HNS unavailability.
- KubeProxy incorrectly interpreted these failures as the LoadBalancer being absent and reset the internal LoadBalancer ID/state.

However, the actual HNS LoadBalancer objects were never deleted. After HNS restarted, the LoadBalancers were restored through the HNS backup/restore (rehydration) mechanism.
Later, when KubeProxy attempted to recreate the same LoadBalancer/frontend configuration, the operation failed because the LoadBalancer already existed in HNS.

### What did you expect to happen?

KubeProxy should treat HNS unavailability as a transient failure and avoid resetting/deleting LoadBalancer state when HNS APIs are temporarily inaccessible.
KubeProxy should:

- Distinguish transient HNS communication failures from actual “LoadBalancer not found” conditions.
- Retry reconciliation after HNS becomes healthy instead of assuming LoadBalancer absence.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Kubernetes Service backed by a deployment with 8 pods.
2. Continuously restart HNS in a loop with a 100 ms sleep interval (100 iterations).
3. Simultaneously scale the deployment up and down in a loop with a 100 ms sleep interval (100 iterations).

labels.name: kind/bug

items.body:
__What happened?__

When running kube-proxy in `mode: nftables`, if any Service causes kube-proxy to generate an nftables comment exceeding the Linux kernel's 128-character limit, __the entire nftables transaction is rejected and no service routing rules are applied on that sync cycle__. kube-proxy retries every 30 seconds and fails every time until the offending Service is removed. During this time, __all ClusterIP routing is broken cluster-wide__, including kube-dns.

__How to reproduce__

1. Run a cluster with kube-proxy in `mode: nftables` (recommended default since Kubernetes 1.35)
2. Create a Service where the combined kube-proxy comment string `<namespace>/<service-name>:<port-name>` exceeds 128 characters

A realistic example:

- Namespace: `loft-acme-platform-services-team-dev-v-shared-workloads-ns-001` __(62 chars ✅ valid k8s namespace)__
- Service name: `my-api-svc-x-my-api-namespace-x-acme-shared-vcluster--a1b2c3d4e` __(63 chars ✅ valid k8s service name)__
- kube-proxy comment: `loft-acme-platform-services-team-dev-v-shared-workloads-ns-001/my-api-svc-x-my-api-namespace-x-acme-shared-vcluster--a1b2c3d4e:http` → __131 characters ❌ kernel rejects__

Both the namespace (62 chars) and the service name (63 chars) are individually valid Kubernetes DNS labels (≤63 chars each) and are accepted by the Kubernetes API. It is only the __combined string that kube-proxy constructs for the nftables comment__ — `<namespace>/<name>:<port>` — that exceeds the 128-char kernel limit.

This scenario occurs naturally with tools like __vCluster__, which syncs virtual-cluster Services to the host namespace using the pattern `<svc>-x-<ns>-x-<vcluster>--<hash>`. vCluster correctly truncates the service name to ≤63 chars per Kubernetes spec. However, when combined with a long management namespace name (e.g. `loft-<team>-<env>-v-<vcluster>`), the resulting nftables comment string can exceed 128 characters.

__What you expected to happen__

kube-proxy should either:

- Truncate the nftables comment to ≤128 characters (or omit it entirely) and continue syncing all other service rules successfully, OR
- Skip only the offending Service and continue applying rules for all others

__What actually happened__

kube-proxy logs show the following error on every sync attempt (every 30 seconds):

```javascript
E proxier.go:1788] "nftables sync failed" err=<
    /dev/stdin:1473:84-216: Error: comment too long, 128 characters maximum allowed
    add element ip kube-proxy no-endpoint-services { 10.96.1.100 . tcp . 80 comment "loft-acme-platform-services-team-dev-v-shared-workloads-ns-001/my-api-svc-x-my-api-namespace-x-acme-shared-vcluster--a1b2c3d4e:http" : goto reject-chain }
                                                                                     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
 > ipFamily="IPv4"
I proxier.go:1143] "Sync failed" ipFamily="IPv4" retryingTime="30s"
```

The sync fails __atomically__ — nftables applies rules in a single transaction, so one bad comment causes the __entire ruleset to be rejected__. This means zero ClusterIP routing rules exist on any node during the failure window.

__Impact__

- All Kubernetes Services become unreachable via ClusterIP on all nodes simultaneously
- `kube-dns` ClusterIP is unreachable → DNS stops working for all pods cluster-wide
- Workloads that depend on DNS (e.g. StatefulSets using headless service DNS for peer discovery such as etcd HA clusters) cannot initialize
- The failure is silent from a pod perspective — packets are dropped, not refused with an error
- Only removing the offending Service restores normal operation

__Kubernetes version__

```javascript
Server Version: v1.35.0
```

__kube-proxy mode__

```yaml
mode: nftables
```

__OS / kernel__

Talos Linux, kernel 6.x (nftables native mode)

__Suggested fix__

The nftables comment is purely for human readability — it has no functional effect on routing. The fix should be straightforward: __truncate comment strings to ≤128 characters__ before including them in nftables statements. The iptables proxier does not have this issue.

items.body:
### What happened? Our production clusters run kube-proxy in `ipvs` mode. We evaluated migrating to `nftables` mode and observed that `kube-proxy` takes a long time to complete a sync, with the `nft` process at 100% CPU for most of that time. This looks related to [#135639](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/135639), which was addressed in v1.36. We are testing on v1.36.1 and still see multi-minute syncs. The two dominant costs we measure are: 1. the `ListAll` (`nft --json --terse list table ip kube-proxy`) that runs on every sync, including incremental syncs, and 1. the full sync re-emitting the entire table even when almost nothing changed. #### How we measured We created different numbers of Services/EndpointSlices in a test cluster and read kube-proxy logs at `--v=2`. A sync logs three lines: ``` I0529 17:51:15.687847 1 proxier.go:1094] "Syncing nftables rules" ipFamily="IPv4" fullSync=true I0529 17:52:18.984398 1 proxier.go:1712] "Reloading service nftables data" ipFamily="IPv4" numServices=44125 numEndpoints=44152 I0529 18:07:59.283867 1 proxier.go:1088] "SyncProxyRules complete" ipFamily="IPv4" elapsed="16m43.895505566s" ``` - ListAll time is roughly the gap between `"Syncing nftables rules"` and `"Reloading service nftables data"`. During this window `nft --json --terse list table ip kube-proxy` runs at 100% CPU. (This window also includes a small stale-chain delete transaction, which is negligible at these scales.) - Total time is the `elapsed=` value on `"SyncProxyRules complete"`. #### Test environment - Instance: `m6a.4xlarge` - kube-proxy: v1.36.1, `mode: nftables`. Default sync params: `minSyncPeriod=1s syncPeriod=30s maxSyncPeriod=1h0m0s`. - calico-node: v3.31.3 - Kernel: Linux 7.0 (Ubuntu 26.04); also reproduced on Linux 7.1-rc4 - Control plane: v1.33.7 - kubelet: v1.33.7 > We ran kube-proxy v1.36.1, despite the version skew against the v1.33.7 control plane and kubelet, to include the v1.36 nftables improvements (#135800, #136499). We believe the behavior we measured does not depend on the control plane or kubelet version: it is node-local nftables programming, driven only by the number of Services/EndpointSlices. If that assumption is wrong, please let us know and we can re-test on a version-matched cluster. Our production clusters reach ~44k Services at an almost 1:1 Service-to-endpoint ratio. That is a much larger Service count than #135639's repro (~1k–5k Services, with high endpoints-per-Service). So the cost here is driven by the number of Services/chains, not just endpoint fan-out, and it appears at Service counts well beyond what #135639 tested. No production workloads run on the test cluster. To trigger incremental syncs, a script creates and deletes 50 Services every 30 seconds. #### Results `fullSync=true` (full sync) vs `fullSync=false` (incremental). Each cell is the p50 across the collected syncs at that scale; the ListAll and Total values are taken from the same sync (the one at p50 of Total). | N (services ~ endpoints) | incremental — ListAll | incremental — Total | full — ListAll | full — Total | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 4,125 | 874 ms | 878 ms | 939 ms | 5.11 s | | 14,125 | 7.25 s | 7.49 s | 7.45 s | 58.25 s | | 24,125 | 20.44 s | 20.76 s | 21.48 s | 3m11.10s | | 34,125 | 39.61 s | 40.30 s | 47.19 s | 8m13.51s | | 44,125 | 1m9.01s | 1m10.14s | 1m3.30s | 16m43.90s | | 44,125 (empty kube-proxy table) | — | — | 284 ms | 4m46.84s | Observations: - From 4k to 44k Services (~11× the count), incremental sync grew ~80× and full sync grew ~197×. The growth is much steeper than linear in the number of Services. - Incremental sync is almost entirely `ListAll`. The actual write is small (<2s even at 44k); the rest is reading the whole table to discover existing chains/affinity sets for cleanup. - Full sync = `ListAll` + re-emitting the whole table. At 44k, ListAll is ~63s of the 16m43s; the remaining ~15.5m is the kernel reprocessing the full set of chains/rules during the commit. - A freshly created node (empty `kube-proxy` table) does a full sync in ~4m47s, which is _faster_ than the hourly full sync on a populated table (~16m43s). This suggests the kernel cost during commit scales with how much already exists in the table, not just with how much is being written. ### What did you expect to happen? Sync time grows too fast with Service count. We don't necessarily expect constant-time syncs, but the current growth means a single change at 44k Services already costs more than a minute (incremental) and the hourly full sync costs ~16 minutes. We'd like both to be substantially lower. #### Incremental sync At 44k Services, an incremental sync takes >1 minute, so any single change (Service create, deployment rollout) has a Network Programming Latency (NPL) over a minute on that node. This is too slow for our production use case. We would like incremental NPL to be on the order of seconds (e.g. p50 ~30s or better) at this scale. Incremental sync calls `ListAll` (reads existing chains and affinity sets) on every run. Could kube-proxy keep an in-memory copy of the committed state and skip `ListAll` on incremental syncs? All writes to the nftables table go through transactions, and in normal operation nothing else modifies kube-proxy's table, so trusting the in-memory copy seems safe, with a periodic full sync as the reconciliation/safety net. #### Full sync Full sync runs at kube-proxy startup and every hour. At 44k, a full sync takes ~16m. During that window the data plane keeps working on the previously committed rules, but any Service/EndpointSlice change that arrives during the full sync is not reflected on the node until the full sync finishes. NPL can spike to ~16m once per hour. We would like the hourly full sync to be ~1m at p50 at this scale. The first full sync at startup taking longer is acceptable. Today full sync writes all Service/EndpointSlice data from the informer to nftables regardless of whether it already matches the kernel. Could full sync use its `ListAll` result to diff actual vs desired state and write only the differences? ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? We use [https://github.com/haojiwu/k8s-scale-test](https://github.com/haojiwu/k8s-scale-test) to create synthetic Services + EndpointSlices: ``` # Create ~44k Services, each with 1 synthetic endpoint. # (apiserver-bound; takes a while to create all objects.) KUBE_CONTEXT= ./k8s-scale-test.sh load 44125 # Continuously create/delete Services to trigger incremental syncs. KUBE_CONTEXT= ./k8s-scale-test.sh churn ``` Then restart the kube-proxy pod and read the new pod's logs: - the first sync after pod creation is a full sync (`fullSync=true`) - subsequent syncs driven by churn are incremental (`fullSync=false`) We also reproduced on a Linux 7.1-rc4 kernel; results are similar. ### Anything else we need to know? _No response_ ### Kubernetes version
```console $ kubectl version Client Version: v1.34.0 Kustomize Version: v5.7.1 Server Version: v1.33.7 ```

Self managed cluster on AWS EC2

labels.name: kind/bug

items.body:
### What happened?

When kube-proxy is configured to use IPVS with the `mh` (Maglev Hashing) scheduler, traffic may fail during endpoint transitions when some backend destinations become unavailable.

The issue happens because IPVS `mh` preserves `last_weight` internally even after a destination weight is updated to `0`. As a result, the Maglev lookup table may still contain references to destinations that are no longer eligible to receive traffic.

Without the `mh-fallback` flag enabled, IPVS may fail to select another healthy destination and instead return:

```text
no destination available
```

This can lead to transient traffic failures during pod termination, rolling updates, endpoint churn, or similar scenarios where backend availability changes dynamically.

A proposed fix was implemented in the following PR:

* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138688

The PR enables `FlagFallBack` together with `FlagSourceHash` for the `mh` scheduler in kube-proxy IPVS mode.


### What did you expect to happen?

When a destination becomes unavailable (for example, weight becomes `0` during pod termination), IPVS using the `mh` scheduler should fall back to another healthy backend destination instead of returning `no destination available`.

Traffic disruption should be minimized during endpoint transitions and rolling updates.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Kubernetes cluster with kube-proxy running in IPVS mode.

2. Configure kube-proxy to use the `mh` scheduler.

3. Deploy a Service with multiple backend Pods.

4. Generate traffic that consistently hashes to a specific backend.

5. Terminate or make one of the backend Pods unavailable so that its weight becomes `0`.

6. Observe that some requests may fail with behavior corresponding to:

```text
no destination available
```

7. Observe IPVS state during the transition:

```bash
ipvsadm -Ln --stats
ipvsadm -Ln --persistent
```

The issue is related to the Maglev lookup table still referencing destinations whose effective weight is no longer usable.

A proposed fix is available here:

* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138688


### Anything else we need to know?

This issue appears to be specific to the interaction between Kubernetes kube-proxy IPVS mode and Linux IPVS `mh` scheduler behavior.

The Linux kernel implementation preserves `last_weight`, which may cause stale destination references to remain in the Maglev lookup table during transitions.

Enabling the IPVS `mh-fallback` behavior allows IPVS to select another healthy backend when the originally selected destination is unavailable.

Related PR:

* https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138688

@npinaeva had done some nftables scaling testing a while back and determined that nftables kube-proxy startup time was much slower than iptables kube-proxy startup time. 

#130119 fixed this for the _restart_ case (kube-proxy starting up when there's already a mostly-correct ruleset present and we just need to synchronize to make sure we get any changes that happened while kube-proxy wasn't running), but it didn't address the "cold start" case. In particular, when adding a new node to a large cluster, kube-proxy on that node will have to sync the entire ruleset starting from nothing.

It's possible that #135800 and #136499 may have fixed this... we hadn't gotten as far as debugging _exactly_ what made things slow.

So part 1 is: see if starting up a fresh kube-proxy in a large cluster (lots of services and endpoints) is still slow (either in general, or specifically compared to the iptables backend).

If it turns out we do still need improvements, part 2 is to do that. One thing to try is splitting the transaction up into multiple steps rather than adding every single new service and endpoint all at once. In particular, if we are starting from a state where the `kube-proxy` table does not yet exist, then:

- The endpoint chains and affinity sets can be created first, potentially split up into multiple transactions if there are a lot of them.
- The service chains can be created next, potentially split up into multiple transactions if there are a lot of them.
- Once all the service chains exist, we can fill in all the service sets and maps. Again, at least in theory, this could be split up into multiple transactions, though I'm not sure if that would have better or worse performance.

items.body: ### What would you like to be added? An opt-in annotation that tells kube-proxy to skip installing REJECT/DROP rules in the filter table (`KUBE-EXTERNAL-SERVICES`) for a Service's external IPs when no endpoints exist on that node. For example: ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: ntp-anycast annotations: projectcalico.org/loadBalancerIPs: '["1.2.3.4"]' service.kubernetes.io/no-reject-on-no-endpoints: "true" <<< spec: type: LoadBalancer externalTrafficPolicy: Local ports: - name: ntp protocol: UDP port: 123 targetPort: 1123 selector: app: chrony status: loadBalancer: ingress: - ip: 1.2.3.4 # anycast VIP advertised via BGP ipMode: VIP ``` When `no-reject-on-no-endpoints: "true"` is set and no local endpoints exist, kube-proxy would not install the filter rule. Traffic would fall through to normal kernel routing, where the BGP speaker (or similar) handles failover. This allows BGP/anycast deployments to rely on routing failover to a nearby cluster/region. ### Why is this needed? kube-proxy installs filter rules in `KUBE-EXTERNAL-SERVICES` to REJECT or DROP traffic to external IPs when no endpoints are available. This is correct for standard Services — it gives clients an immediate ICMP error instead of a timeout. However, in BGP/anycast deployments this behavior prevents routing failover. The BGP speaker withdraws the route when endpoints disappear, so the kernel routing table would naturally send the packet off-node. But kube-proxy's filter rule intercepts and drops the packet before routing takes effect. Example topology: When local service is working: ```shell › kubectl get endpointslices ntp-anycast-t7n2l NAME ADDRESSTYPE PORTS ENDPOINTS ntp-anycast-t7n2l IPv4 123 100.90.14.133 ``` Output from the node in `Cluster A` with respective pod running: ```shell # iptables-save | grep 1.2.3.4 -A KUBE-SERVICES -d 1.2.3.4/32 -p udp -m comment --comment "test/ntp-anycast:ntp-udp-123 loadbalancer IP" -m udp --dport 123 -j KUBE-EXT-IL6URECE27T65EPH ``` Other node in same cluster `Cluster A` (e.g. with pods consuming this service): ```shell # iptables-save | grep 1.2.3.4 -A KUBE-SERVICES -d 1.2.3.4/32 -p udp -m comment --comment "test/ntp-anycast:ntp-udp-123 loadbalancer IP" -m udp --dport 123 -j KUBE-EXT-IL6URECE27T65EPH -A KUBE-EXTERNAL-SERVICES -d 1.2.3.4/32 -p udp -m comment --comment "test/ntp-anycast:ntp-udp-123 has no local endpoints" -m udp --dport 123 -j DROP ``` When local service fails, we expect a fallback to another region. ```shell › kubectl get endpointslices ntp-anycast-t7n2l NAME ADDRESSTYPE PORTS ENDPOINTS ntp-anycast-t7n2l IPv4 123 ``` Output any node in `Cluster A`: ```shell # iptables-save | grep 1.2.3.4 -A KUBE-EXTERNAL-SERVICES -d 1.2.3.4/32 -p udp -m comment --comment "test/ntp-anycast:ntp-udp-123 has no endpoints" -m udp --dport 123 -j REJECT --reject-with icmp-port-unreachable ``` Due to above rule: - Nodes in `Cluster A` are able to communicate with `1.2.3.4/32` service in `Cluster 2` - Pods in `Cluster A` are *not* able to communicate with `1.2.3.4/32` service in `Cluster 2` and get `connection refused` error message This proposed approach would follow the existing annotation-based extension pattern used by Service features such as `service.kubernetes.io/topology-mode` and load balancer source ranges. Use cases: anycast UDP services, anycast ingress, and active-active multi-cluster Services with shared VIPs. /sig network /kind feature /area kube-proxy

In the past, we had relied upon the metrics `kube_apiserver_clusterip_allocator_available_ips` and `kube_apiserver_clusterip_allocator_allocation_errors_total` to get notified when we are running out of IP addresses. This no longer works because these metrics are now gone.

My understanding is that we are now in the world of `MultiCIDRServiceAllocator` and KEP 1880. According to https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-network/1880-multiple-service-cidrs/README.md#monitoring-requirements it should still produce these metrics (or am I reading this wrong?).

### What did you expect to happen?

The metrics `kube_apiserver_clusterip_allocator_available_ips` and `kube_apiserver_clusterip_allocator_allocation_errors_total` should still be available.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I guess you would have to do the same dance we did:

1. Create a new `ServiceCidr` which is a superset of the existing `kubernetes` one created/managed by kube-apiserver
2. Adjust the `--service-cluster-ip-range` CLI flag of kube-apiserver to match the newly created `ServiceCidr`
3. Delete the default `ServiceCidr`: `kubectl delete servicecidr kubernetes` so that kube-apiserver re-creates it with new settings
4. Delete the `ServiceCidr` from step 1

Before this dance of extending the `ServiceCidr` we had those metrics. Only after extending/re-creating the default `ServiceCidr` we lost those metrics. We are still seeing metrics for other allocators:

items.body:
### What happened?

The [`decoratedWatcher`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.33.0/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/generic/registry/decorated_watcher.go#L61) calls `d.decorator(recv.Object)` on watch events, but the object dispatched by the [watch cache](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.33.0/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go#L974) is wrapped in a `cachingObject`. Since `cachingObject` implements [`runtime.CacheableObject`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.33.0/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/interfaces.go#L344) but is not the underlying resource type, any decorator that relies on a type assertion silently no-ops for watch events while working correctly for GET and LIST.

For Services, the [`Store.Decorator`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.33.0/pkg/registry/core/service/storage/storage.go#L129) is set to [`defaultOnRead`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.33.0/pkg/registry/core/service/storage/storage.go#L232), which type-switches on `*api.Service` / `*api.ServiceList` to call [`defaultOnReadService`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.33.0/pkg/registry/core/service/storage/storage.go#L256). This defaults `spec.ipFamilies` (via [`defaultOnReadIPFamilies`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.33.0/pkg/registry/core/service/storage/storage.go#L280)), normalizes `spec.clusterIPs`, and drops `spec.internalTrafficPolicy` for ExternalName services. None of this runs for watch events because the `*cachingObject` wrapper falls through the type switch to the [default no-op case](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.33.0/pkg/registry/core/service/storage/storage.go#L238).

The immediate consequence observed is a KCM endpoint controller [panic](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.33.0/pkg/controller/endpoint/endpoints_controller.go#L223) (`index out of range [0] with length 0` at `svc.Spec.IPFamilies[0]`) when processing services stored in etcd without `ipFamilies` (created before dual-stack GA ~v1.23).

### What did you expect to happen?

Watch events should deliver objects with the same defaulted fields as GET/LIST responses. The `decoratedWatcher` should unwrap `CacheableObject` before calling the decorator so that type-assertion work consistently across all read paths.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a kind cluster (v1.33+)
2. Create a ClusterIP Service with a selector and matching pods
3. Strip `spec.ipFamilies` from the Service in etcd using [auger](https://github.com/etcd-io/auger) (simulates a pre-dualstack-GA service object)
4. Verify `kubectl get svc` still shows `ipFamilies: ["IPv4"]` the GET decorator masks the missing field
5. Trigger a status-only update: `kubectl patch svc <name> --subresource=status -p '{"status":{"conditions":[{"type":"Test","status":"True"}]}}'`
6. Observe: the watch event delivered to KCM has no `ipFamilies`, and the endpoint controller panics

A spec update (e.g., `kubectl annotate svc`) does NOT trigger the issue because the Service allocator runs during spec updates and backfills `ipFamilies` into etcd. Status updates bypass the allocator entirely.

### Anything else we need to know?

## Root cause:
The watch dispatch path wraps objects in `cachingObject` via [`setCachingObjects()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.33.0/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go#L913) for serialization caching (called from [`dispatchEvent()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.33.0/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/cacher.go#L944)). When `decoratedWatcher.run()` calls `d.decorator(recv.Object)`, the decorator receives a `*cachingObject` instead of the underlying type (e.g., `*api.Service`). The Service decorator's [type switch](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.33.0/pkg/registry/core/service/storage/storage.go#L233) falls through to the default no-op case.

### Discussion: where should the unwrapping live?
There are two options for where to unwrap the `CacheableObject` and apply the decorator:
**Option A: Unwrap in `decoratedWatcher` (apiserver layer)**

Before calling `d.decorator()`, check if the object implements `CacheableObject`. If so, call `GetObject()` to get a deep copy, decorate it, and replace `recv.Object`. This fixes the issue systemically for all resource types and all decorators.

Trade-off: `GetObject()` performs a deep copy on every watch event in the apiserver, which has a performance cost at scale. This needs benchmarking.

**Option B: Unwrap at the component level (e.g., KCM)**

Components that consume watch events would type-assert to `CacheableObject`, call `GetObject()` to unwrap, and then apply the necessary defaulting themselves. This moves the deep-copy overhead out of the apiserver and into the individual consumers that actually need the unwrapped object.

Trade-off: each component needs to be aware that watch events may arrive wrapped, and handle the unwrapping but it avoids adding deep-copy cost to the apiserver's hot path.

I'd like SIG API Machinery's input on the preferred approach. I'm planning to submit a defensive fix for the KCM endpoint controller in parallel as an immediate mitigation, and can work on either option for the systemic fix.

# DRA Granular Status Authorization: Migration Guide

Starting in Kubernetes v1.36, the `DRAResourceClaimGranularStatusAuthorization` feature gate
(beta, on-by-default) enforces fine-grained authorization checks for `ResourceClaim` status
updates. Components that previously only needed `update`/`patch` on `resourceclaims/status`
now require additional permissions on **synthetic subresources** depending on which status
fields they modify.

Reference: #134947, https://github.com/kubernetes/website/pull/55070

---

## What changed

| Old permission | New additional permission required | Who needs it |
|---|---|---|
| `resourceclaims/status` `update`/`patch` | `resourceclaims/binding` `update`/`patch` | Schedulers, allocation controllers (anything modifying `status.allocation` or `status.reservedFor`) |
| `resourceclaims/status` `update`/`patch` | `resourceclaims/driver` `associated-node:update`/`associated-node:patch` | Node-local DRA drivers (ServiceAccount bound to a specific node via pod-bound token) |
| `resourceclaims/status` `update`/`patch` | `resourceclaims/driver` `arbitrary-node:update`/`arbitrary-node:patch` | Control-plane DRA drivers, network controllers, or any component managing device status across nodes |

The existing `resourceclaims/status` permission is **still required** — it remains the "front door".
The new synthetic subresources are **additional** checks on top of it.

These new permissions can be added **now** in preparation for 1.36, they are inert in earlier versions of Kubernetes.

---

## Migration by component type

### Node-local DRA drivers

These run as DaemonSets with a ServiceAccount whose token is bound to the node (via a pod
scheduled on that node). They update `status.devices` for their own driver.

**Add this rule to the driver's ClusterRole:**

```yaml
- apiGroups: ["resource.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["resourceclaims/driver"]
  verbs: ["associated-node:update", "associated-node:patch"]
  resourceNames: ["<your-driver-name>"]  # e.g. "dra.example.com"
```

**Keep the existing rule:**

```yaml
- apiGroups: ["resource.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["resourceclaims/status"]
  verbs: ["get", "update", "patch"]
```

### Control-plane DRA drivers / multi-node controllers

These run as Deployments (not node-bound). They update `status.devices` for their driver
from a central controller.

**Add this rule to the controller's ClusterRole:**

```yaml
- apiGroups: ["resource.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["resourceclaims/driver"]
  verbs: ["arbitrary-node:update", "arbitrary-node:patch"]
  resourceNames: ["<your-driver-name>"]  # e.g. "dra.example.com"
```

**Keep the existing rule:**

```yaml
- apiGroups: ["resource.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["resourceclaims/status"]
  verbs: ["get", "update", "patch"]
```

### Schedulers

These modify `status.allocation` and `status.reservedFor` when binding claims to nodes.

**Add this rule to the scheduler's ClusterRole:**

```yaml
- apiGroups: ["resource.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["resourceclaims/binding"]
  verbs: ["update", "patch"]
```

**Keep the existing rule:**

```yaml
- apiGroups: ["resource.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["resourceclaims/status"]
  verbs: ["get", "update", "patch"]
```

> Note: The built-in `system:kube-scheduler` ClusterRole is updated automatically
> by the bootstrap policy when the feature gate is enabled. Only custom schedulers
> need manual updates.

### Operators / virtual clusters that proxy all ResourceClaim operations

These need **all** of the above depending on what operations they proxy.

**Add both rules:**

```yaml
- apiGroups: ["resource.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["resourceclaims/binding"]
  verbs: ["update", "patch"]
- apiGroups: ["resource.k8s.io"]
  resources: ["resourceclaims/driver"]
  verbs: ["associated-node:update", "associated-node:patch", "arbitrary-node:update", "arbitrary-node:patch"]
```

### Components that only read status or manage non-status fields

No changes needed. The new checks only apply to **writes** to `status.allocation`,
`status.reservedFor`, and `status.devices`.

---

items.body:
Add support for a `k8s-cidr` format value in the existing `+k8s:format` declarative validation (DV) tag to validate that a string field contains valid CIDR notation (e.g., `192.168.1.0/24` or `2001:db8::/64`). This corresponds to the OpenAPI `format: cidr` keyword.

## Motivation

CIDR notation validation is common across Kubernetes networking APIs (NetworkPolicy, Service CIDR allocation, ClusterCIDR, etc.). OpenAPI supports `format: cidr` as a format. Adding this to DV enables declarative validation of CIDR fields currently validated with handwritten code.

## Kubernetes API Example

**`IPBlock.CIDR`** in `pkg/apis/networking/validation/validation.go`:

```go
// Handwritten validation today:
func ValidateIPBlock(ipb *networking.IPBlock, fldPath *field.Path, opts NetworkPolicyValidationOptions) field.ErrorList {
    allErrs := field.ErrorList{}
    if ipb.CIDR == "" {
        allErrs = append(allErrs, field.Required(fldPath.Child("cidr"), "").MarkCoveredByDeclarative())
        return allErrs
    }
    allErrs = append(allErrs, apivalidation.IsValidCIDRForLegacyField(
        fldPath.Child("cidr"), ipb.CIDR, opts.AllowCIDRsEvenIfInvalid)...)
    _, cidrIPNet, err := netutils.ParseCIDRSloppy(ipb.CIDR)
    // ...
}
```

With the proposed format:

```go
type IPBlock struct {
    // +k8s:required
    // +k8s:format=k8s-cidr
    CIDR string
}
```

## OpenAPI Semantics

- **OpenAPI format:** `cidr`
- **kube-openapi strfmt:** registered in `strfmt/default.go`, validated with `net.ParseCIDR()`
- **Format:** `<ip-address>/<prefix-length>` for both IPv4 and IPv6

## DV Design Considerations

- **Sloppy vs. strict parsing:** Similar to the `k8s-ip` ratcheting concern — existing Kubernetes CIDR fields use `netutils.ParseCIDRSloppy()` which tolerates leading zeros in IP octets. The DV format should use sloppy parsing (e.g., `k8s-cidr` → `CIDRSloppy()`) to match historical behavior. A strict variant could be added later.
- **Relationship to `k8s-ip`:** CIDR validation is closely related to IP validation — a CIDR is an IP address plus prefix length. If `k8s-ip` is blocked on ratcheting concerns, `k8s-cidr` may face the same issue. These should be evaluated together.
- **IPv4/IPv6 variants:** Consider whether to add `k8s-cidrv4` and `k8s-cidrv6` for fields constrained to a specific address family.
- **Naming convention:** Follows existing `k8s-` prefix pattern.

## Implementation Notes

- Should be added to the format switch in `validators/format.go`
- Runtime validation function should use `net.ParseCIDR()` or `netutils.ParseCIDRSloppy()`
- High priority — CIDR is used extensively in NetworkPolicy, Service CIDR allocation, and cluster networking
- Validator file: `staging/src/k8s.io/code-generator/cmd/validation-gen/validators/format.go`

/sig api-machinery
/triage accepted
/area api-validation

See an example below, where my `minSyncPeriod` is set to 14s, and the time between completion of last sync, and start of next sync, is only 12 seconds. BUT, the time between sync-start to sync-start, is the actual 14s minSyncPeriod time.

For unclear reasons, the test was passing when the client-go TLS cache was not GC'd.

_Originally posted by @liggitt in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/136355#discussion_r2956421861_

/assign aojea

Even without the GC change, the following patch could be used to induce a failure in `TestEgressToWebhookWithProxy`:

```diff
diff --git staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/util/webhook/client.go staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/util/webhook/client.go
index 63ea4e2666e..b368dc40af1 100644
--- staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/util/webhook/client.go
+++ staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/util/webhook/client.go
@@ -25,6 +25,7 @@ import (
 	"net/url"
 	"strconv"
 	"strings"
+	"time"

 	"k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime"
 	"k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/schema"
@@ -144,6 +145,13 @@ func (cm *ClientManager) HookClient(cc ClientConfig) (*rest.RESTClient, error) {

 func (cm *ClientManager) hookClientConfig(cc ClientConfig) (*rest.Config, error) {
 	complete := func(cfg *rest.Config) (*rest.Config, error) {
+		if cfg.Dial == nil { // make each config use distinct TLS cache key
+			cfg.Dial = (&net.Dialer{
+				Timeout:   30 * time.Second,
+				KeepAlive: 30 * time.Second,
+			}).DialContext
+		}
+
 		// Avoid client-side rate limiting talking to the webhook backend.
 		// Rate limiting should happen when deciding how many requests to serve.
 		cfg.QPS = -1
```

The above change would induce a cache miss of the client-go TLS cache and the test would fail:

        User-Agent: Go-http-client/1.1

    httpproxy_test.go:246: Webhook was hit as expected
    httpproxy_test.go:253: Proxy was hit, but should have been bypassed by NO_PROXY
```

items.body:
### What would you like to be added?

The Windows kube-proxy (winkernel proxier) currently lacks Prometheus metrics for load balancer operation failures. This makes it difficult to monitor and diagnose LB failures in production Windows clusters.

**Proposed metrics:**

Add three new `ALPHA` stability counter metrics:
- `kubeproxy_sync_proxy_rules_winkernel_lb_create_failures_total` - tracks LB creation failures
- `kubeproxy_sync_proxy_rules_winkernel_lb_update_failures_total` - tracks LB update failures  
- `kubeproxy_sync_proxy_rules_winkernel_lb_delete_failures_total` - tracks LB deletion failures

**Proposed labels for each metric:**

| Label | Values |
|-------|--------|
| `ip_family` | `IPv4`, `IPv6` |
| `lb_type` | `clusterip`, `nodeport`, `externalip`, `ingressip`, `healthcheck` |
| `error` | `network_not_found`, `port_already_exists`, `not_implemented`, `invalid_ip`, `other` |

The maximum cardinality per metric would be 50 (2 × 5 × 5), but in practice much lower since a proxier instance typically uses a single IP family and most error/lb_type combinations never fire.

### Why is this needed?

1. **Observability gap**: Linux kube-proxy modes (iptables, ipvs, nftables) have extensive metrics, but Windows winkernel proxier has none for LB failures.
2. **Production debugging**: Without these metrics, operators have no visibility into HCN/HNS failures until services become unavailable.
3. **Alerting**: Cannot set up proactive alerting on LB failure rates in Windows clusters.
4. **Parity**: Brings Windows kube-proxy closer to feature parity with Linux modes in terms of observability.

### Additional context

Example output from a real AKS Windows node:

```

items.body:
### What happened?

Occasionally on newer Windows Server 2019 OS builds, Windows Pods experience connection timeouts when attempting to access a Kubernetes LoadBalancer VIP that routes back to a pod on the exact same node (hairpinning).
When this issue happened, the `NatPool` for the LoadBalancer policy is incorrectly set to the VIP itself instead of the Node's IP address. Because the backend pod sees the VIP as the source IP, it sends its reply back to the VIP. The Windows virtual switch (HNS) intercepts this reply, treats it as a brand-new inbound LoadBalancer request, and routes it into an infinite loop (or drops it), causing the connection to time out.

### What did you expect to happen?

Pod-to-LB hairpin traffic should always route correctly via a NatPool built with the Node IP.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

It occurs occasionally, so hard to reproduce consistently. 
1. Deploy a LoadBalancer service with local endpoints.
2. Run hnsdiag list loadbalancers on the host. Observe the NatPool uses the External VIP instead of the Node IP because "SourceVip" is "".

### Anything else we need to know?

1. Empty `sourceVip` breaks hairpin routing on newer Windows HNS kernels.
In `pkg/proxy/windows/proxier.go`, `sourceVip` is an empty string "".
```
var sourceVip = proxier.sourceVip
if containsPublicIP || containsNodeIP {
sourceVip = proxier.nodeIP.String()
}
```
When `kube-proxy` passes "" to the Windows Host Compute Network (HCN) API:
* Sometimes (older versions) Windows HNS defaulted an empty SourceVIP to the Node IP. Hairpinning worked.
* Occationally Windows HNS default an empty SourceVIP to the Frontend VIP. Hairpinning breaks due to the routing loop.

items.body:
### What happened?

The issue only occurred after upgrading Windows Server OS 2019 from Build `17763.8027` to Build `17763.8146`. The Windows nodes depends on Windows networking stack, corresponding `kube-proxy` without CNI.

On Windows nodes, when a LoadBalancer or NodePort service has its backing endpoints scaled to 0, `kube-proxy` fails to release the underlying Host Networking Service (HNS) port lock. When endpoints are scaled back up, `kube-proxy` attempts to recreate the policy, hits a collision with the orphaned lock, and enters a crash loop, throwing the following Windows HNS error:
```
proxier.go:1604] "Nodeport policy creation failed" err="hcnCreateLoadBalancer failed in Win32: The specified port already exists. (0x803b0013) {\"Success\":false,\"Error\":\"The sp
ecified port already exists. \",\"ErrorCode\":2151350291}" nodeport=30364 sourceVip="" proxierIPFamily="IPv4" nodeIP="10.0.0.4"
```
This is exposed by a recent OS-level change. On older Windows Server builds (e.g., `17763.8027`), the OS silently forgave the leak and allowed overwriting the inactive policy. On newer strict builds (e.g., `17763.8146`), HNS strictly rejects the overwrite, making explicit cleanup a hard functional requirement.

Also seeing [oad Balancer already exists.](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/proxy/winkernel/proxier.go#L1407) while it is clearly commented as **"//This should not happen"**.

### What did you expect to happen?

`kube-proxy` should successfully delete the old Windows HNS LoadBalancer policy when endpoints drop to 0, freeing the OS port lock, and cleanly recreate the policy when new endpoints are available.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Provision a Kubernetes cluster with a Windows worker node running OS Build `17763.8146` or newer.
2. Deploy a `LoadBalancer` service and a backing deployment (replicas: 1).
3. Scale the deployment to 0: `kubectl scale deployment <name> --replicas=0`.
4. Scale the deployment back to 1: `kubectl scale deployment <name> --replicas=1`.
5. Observe the kube-proxy logs on the Windows node. It will fail with:
`err="hcnCreateLoadBalancer failed in Win32: The specified port already exists. (0x803b0013)`.

### Anything else we need to know?

Restarting the `kube-proxy` pod on the affected node temporarily clears the issue. During its startup synchronization, `kube-proxy` correctly identifies the orphaned HNS LoadBalancers and garbage-collects them. However, the standard runtime sync loop continues to leak them.

This likely exposed a bug in the cleanup logic within `syncProxyRules`, so the NodePort LB remains active in Windows HNS with a lock on the port. When a new Endpoint ID spins up, the hash changes so a new NodePort policy is created, which leads to `0x803b0013`.

### What happened?

While working on a dual-stack issue on `kube-proxy` (#114702 #137370), I discovered another issue.

If the IPv6 support is turned off on a node (for example, with sysctl), kube-proxy fails to correctly detect that the node is single‑stack, and logs the following error when a dual-service is deployed:

```
I0304 09:29:42.889348       1 server.go:265] "kube-proxy running in dual-stack mode" primary ipFamily="IPv4"

$ sudo sysctl -a | grep  net.ipv6.conf.all.disable_ipv6
net.ipv6.conf.all.disable_ipv6 = 1
```
If dual-stack mode is enabled incorrectly, the following error occurs:

```
E0304 09:11:04.154332       1 proxier.go:1777] "Failed to bind service address to dummy device" err="error bind address: fd00:1234::f:d72 to interface: kube-ipvs0, err: permission denied" ipFamily="IPv6" serviceName="default/nginx-dual"
E0304 09:11:04.154358       1 proxier.go:1066] "Failed to sync service" err="error bind address: fd00:1234::f:d72 to interface: kube-ipvs0, err: permission denied" ipFamily="IPv6" servicePortName="default/nginx-dual" virtualServer="[fd00:1234::f:d72]:8080/TCP"

```

### What did you expect to happen?

Dual-stack support should not be enabled, and the following message should be logged instead:

`I0304 11:24:11.226354       1 server.go:267] "kube-proxy running in single-stack mode" ipFamily="IPv4"`

The problem is on these lines: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/bd3c97fbd8d79741ba71f85a1eb342c01266e2b9/cmd/kube-proxy/app/server_linux.go#L107-L112 -- they do not take into account whether IPv6 support has been disabled. This option has existed since Linux kernel v2.6.27.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

* Deploy a multi-node, dual-stack Kubernetes cluster.
* Disable IPv6 on one node: `sudo sysctl -w net.ipv6.conf.all.disable_ipv6=1`
* Deploy a Service that requests both address families.
* Observe how `kube-proxy` logs the error.

### What happened?

kube-proxy iptables mode sync latency is 5-6x slower on aws-k8s-1.34 nodes compared to aws-k8s-1.32/1.33 nodes.

  Test environment: Same EKS cluster , same kube-proxy version (v1.34.3-eksbuild.2), same workload (877 services, 2057 endpoints).

  Root cause: aws-k8s-1.34 switched from legacy iptables to iptables-nft (nftables kernel backend with iptables compatibility layer). Every iptables operation is now translated to nftables, adding significant overhead.

  Evidence from the nodes:
  # aws-k8s-1.32 (fast)
  $ iptables --version

  lrwxrwxrwx. 1 root root 17 Jan 23 01:35 /usr/sbin/iptables-nft -> xtables-nft-multi

kube-proxy running in iptables mode should have similar rule sync performance on aws-k8s-1.34 nodes as on aws-k8s-1.32/1.33 nodes

Hi, I have a use-case for a controller that will update the pod status fields used by Pod spec readinessGates configurations.

As a platform owner, part of my responsibility is to prevent users from shooting themselves in the foot. If they fail to configure their pod spec with readiness and startup probes, their pods might be marked ready and added to the service endpoints too soon before other things beyond the user's control are fully ready to serve traffic. I'd like to have the ability to put an object in their namespace that can configure health checks against cluster objects or internal or external endpoints and update the pod status fields used by the deployment's readiness gates.

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: ReadinessGate
metadata:

        matchLabels:
          app.kubernetes.io/name: my-app
```

For this example, my user has a deployment in some namespace which has the label `app.kubernetes.io/name: my-app`. Additionally, I as the platform admin have a deployment in the `my-ingress` namespace with the label `app.kubernetes.io/name: my-ingress` and I'm configuring a health check in the user's namespace that verifies the `readyReplicas` field on the ingress deployment is greater than or equal to 3. If it is, then the pod status conditions should have a readiness gate related `status.conditions` field with the reason `ingressControllerHealthy` added with the new condition's `status` key set to true, and otherwise it should have that field added with the `status` key set to false.

This way, I can ask the users to simply configure a pod readiness gate at their leisure to make use of the newly available fields in pod status, without needing to ask users to modify their apps nor needing build my own controller to add the pod status fields necessary to make use of the readiness gates feature.

items.body:
### What happened?

Kubelet's HTTP readiness/liveness probe follows 301 redirects that change the scheme from HTTP to HTTPS, even when the pod spec explicitly sets `scheme: HTTP`. This causes probes to fail with TLS errors against HTTP-only servers.

The `RedirectChecker` in `pkg/probe/http/http.go` only validates that the redirect hostname matches the original request, but does not validate that the scheme remains unchanged:

```go
// pkg/probe/http/http.go - current code
func RedirectChecker(followNonLocalRedirects bool) func(*http.Request, []*http.Request) error {
    if followNonLocalRedirects {
        return nil
    }
    return func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
        if req.URL.Hostname() != via[0].URL.Hostname() {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        }
        if len(via) >= 10 {
            return errors.New("stopped after 10 redirects")
        }
        return nil  // BUG: Allows scheme changes (HTTP→HTTPS)
    }
}
```

When a server redirects `http://10.42.0.6:8000/health` → `https://10.42.0.6:8000/health` (same hostname, different scheme), the redirect is allowed. The Go HTTP client then attempts a TLS handshake against the HTTP-only server, which fails.

**Kubelet events show the scheme switch:**
```
Warning  Unhealthy  46s  kubelet  Readiness probe failed: Get "http://10.42.0.33:8000/health": connection refused
Warning  Unhealthy  6s   kubelet  Readiness probe failed: Get "https://10.42.0.33:8000/health": EOF
```

**Container logs confirm TLS handshake attempts:**
```
HTTP -> 301 https://10.42.0.33:8000/health
HTTPS DETECTED! TLS ClientHello: 16030105ba01000566
HTTP -> 301 https://10.42.0.33:8000/health
HTTPS DETECTED! TLS ClientHello: 16030105ba01000566
```

Each probe correctly starts with HTTP (from pod spec), but follows the redirect to HTTPS, fails, and repeats indefinitely. The pod never becomes Ready.


### What did you expect to happen?

When a user specifies `scheme: HTTP` in the probe configuration, kubelet should **not** follow redirects that change the scheme to HTTPS. The redirect should be blocked (returning `http.ErrUseLastResponse`), and the probe should succeed with the 301 status code (which is in the 200-399 success range per documentation).

This matches the existing behavior for cross-host redirects, which are correctly blocked.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

**1. Create `redirect_server.py`** - simulates Django's `SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT`:
```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
from http.server import HTTPServer, BaseHTTPRequestHandler
import sys, time

class RedirectHandler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        host = self.headers.get("Host", "localhost:8000")
        https_url = f"https://{host}{self.path}"
        self.send_response(301)
        self.send_header("Location", https_url)
        self.send_header("Content-Length", "0")
        self.end_headers()
        print(f"HTTP -> 301 {https_url}", file=sys.stderr)

    def log_message(self, *args): pass

    def handle(self):
        try:
            self.raw_requestline = self.rfile.readline(65537)
            if self.raw_requestline and self.raw_requestline[0] == 0x16:
                print(f"HTTPS DETECTED! TLS: {self.raw_requestline[:10].hex()}", file=sys.stderr)
                return
            if not self.raw_requestline or not self.parse_request():
                return
            getattr(self, "do_" + self.command, lambda: None)()
            self.wfile.flush()
        except: pass

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("Startup delay 15s...", file=sys.stderr)
    time.sleep(15)
    HTTPServer(("0.0.0.0", 8000), RedirectHandler).serve_forever()
```

**2. Create `Dockerfile`:**
```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim
COPY redirect_server.py /app/
CMD ["python3", "-u", "/app/redirect_server.py"]
```

**3. Create `deployment.yaml`:**
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: probe-redirect-bug
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: probe-redirect-bug}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: probe-redirect-bug}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: server
        image: probe-redirect-bug:latest
        imagePullPolicy: Never
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8000
            scheme: HTTP  # Ignored when server redirects to HTTPS
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
          failureThreshold: 30
```

**4. Deploy and observe:**
```bash
docker build -t probe-redirect-bug:latest .
# For k3s:
docker save probe-redirect-bug:latest | sudo k3s ctr images import -
# For other clusters, push to a registry

kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl get events -w --field-selector reason=Unhealthy
```

[redirect_server.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/25024894/redirect_server.py)
[deployment.yaml](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/25024895/deployment.yaml)
[README.md](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/25024897/README.md)

### Anything else we need to know?

### Real-World Impact

This affects Django applications with `SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT = True`, a common production security setting. Django redirects `http://HOST/...` → `https://HOST/...` using the request's Host header, which means the redirect hostname matches the original request.

### Proposed Fix

Add a scheme check to `RedirectChecker`:

```go
func RedirectChecker(followNonLocalRedirects bool) func(*http.Request, []*http.Request) error {
    if followNonLocalRedirects {
        return nil
    }
    return func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
        orig := via[0].URL
        // Block cross-host OR cross-scheme redirects
        if req.URL.Hostname() != orig.Hostname() || req.URL.Scheme != orig.Scheme {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        }
        if len(via) >= 10 {
            return errors.New("stopped after 10 redirects")
        }
        return nil
    }
}
```

### What would you like to be added?

Today we make assumptions around the Pod IP address coming back from the PodSandboxStatus RPC. This RPC is responsible for returning the ip addresses to the kubelet. The assumptions we make around the current handling of pod ip addresses from containerd and crio, while they do some validation if the pod ip address exists, it possible to return an empty string as the pod ip address. It probably makes sense to do validation in the SyncPod function (link below) to ensure this scenario cannot happen. The function should fail, right now the pod is constantly scheduled without a useful error message. 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/4b5e40aacd021aa1485d29c4965893b3de017697/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L1596

Without any validation, its possible for a pod to come up and have no ip address from the K8s perspective.

items.body:
### What happened?

I tried to create a new service to expose kube-dns on another IP.
It seems to be impossible as it says that the clusterIP (10.96.0.11) I set in the service is already allocated, even if it's not.
Below you'll find the smallest possible process to reproduce this problem.

Interestingly, if I create a service without specifying IP, an IP will be automatically allocated without any problem. I can then delete the service, the IP will be deleted, and if I create the same service but with this specific IP, it will work.
It means that IP are correctly de-allocated when I remove a service.

### What did you expect to happen?

Service to be created with specified IP.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

test-svc.yaml
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  labels:
  name: test
  namespace: kube-system
spec:
  clusterIP: 10.96.0.11
  clusterIPs:
    - 10.96.0.11
    - fd00::b
  internalTrafficPolicy: Cluster
  ipFamilies:
    - IPv4
    - IPv6

  ports:
  - name: dns
    port: 53
    protocol: UDP
    targetPort: 53
  - name: dns-tcp
    port: 53
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 53
  - name: metrics
    port: 9153
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 9153
  selector:
    k8s-app: kube-dns
  sessionAffinity: None
  type: ClusterIP
```

  name: 10.96.0.11

labels.name: kind/bug

items.body:
### What happened?

When I add a port with a duplicate port number but different protocol (UDP instead of TCP) to an existing Deployment, one of these two ports get removed.

### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect both to be present.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Apply this:

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: test-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: test
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: test
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: test
        image: busybox
        command:
        - sleep
        - infinity
        ports:
        - containerPort: 1000
          protocol: TCP
```

Then `kubectl edit` the `Deployment`, duplicating the containerport, but with UDP, like this:

```
        ports:
        - containerPort: 1000
          protocol: TCP
        - containerPort: 1000
          protocol: UDP
```

And you'll observe that one of the two ports is gone in the `Deployment`.

### Anything else we need to know?

There are no mutating webhooks involved. Even with all hooks removed, I still observ this.

When you `get deploy -o yaml`, edit the yaml, `apply --server-side -f /the/yaml`, it does seem to get applied.

My guess is it is due to (only) `containerPort` being the merge key in types.go.

This is very similar to #105610, but that issue is about `Services`.

### Kubernetes version

I've observed this in 1.34.2, 1.33.6 and 1.32.4

### Cloud provider

self hosted Talos

items.body:
### What happened?

The cloud-provider service controller doesn't trigger reconciliation when a LoadBalancer Service's status is cleared by external controllers like GitOps tools. This happens when the Service spec includes `loadBalancerIP` and the GitOps tool updates the Service, clearing the status field. Even though the cloud load balancer continues to function normally, the Service shows a pending status indefinitely because the controller only detects changes to the Service spec, not the status.

### What did you expect to happen?

When a LoadBalancer Service's status is cleared during a resource update, the service controller should detect this change and reconcile by querying the cloud provider to restore the correct LoadBalancer ingress information.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a LoadBalancer Service with `loadBalancerIP` specified in the spec:
   ```yaml
   apiVersion: v1
   kind: Service
   metadata:
     name: test-service
   spec:
     type: LoadBalancer
     loadBalancerIP: 10.50.71.131
     ports:
     - port: 80
   ```
2. Verify the Service has `Status.LoadBalancer.Ingress` populated with the LB IP
3. Apply the same Service YAML using a GitOps tool or kubectl, which clears the status field
4. Observe the Service status remains empty/pending even though the cloud load balancer exists and functions correctly

### Anything else we need to know?

The `needsUpdate()` function in `staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/service/controller.go` (lines 557-616) only checks `Service.Spec` fields like ports, annotations, and IPs. It doesn't check if `Service.Status.LoadBalancer.Ingress` has been cleared.

items.body:
### What happened?

When upgrading a Kubernetes cluster from v1.32 to v1.33 by creating new control plane nodes with v1.33 manifests, the kube-apiserver fails to start with admission errors. 
```
0115 20:56:16.106534   # log start
...
E0115 20:56:24.741991       1 repairip.go:372] "Unhandled Error" err="the ClusterIP [IPv4]: 10.211.95.185 for Service <namespace foo>/<service bar>is not allocated; repairing" logger="UnhandledError"
...
Trace[295533714]: ---"Write to database call failed" len:247,err:ipaddresses.networking.k8s.io "10.211.95.185" is forbidden: not yet ready to handle request 10000ms (20:56:34.744)
Trace[295533714]: [10.000527316s] [10.000527316s] END
E0115 20:56:34.745027       1 repairip.go:235] "Unhandled Error" err="ipaddresses.networking.k8s.io \"10.211.95.185\" is forbidden: not yet ready to handle request" logger="UnhandledError"
I0115 20:56:34.746095       1 repairip.go:236] Shutting down ipallocator-repair-controller
I0115 20:56:34.834949       1 healthz.go:280] informer-sync,poststarthook/start-service-ip-repair-controllers check failed: readyz
[-]informer-sync failed: 4 informers not started yet: [*v1.Pod *v1.ServiceAccount *v1.Secret *v1.Namespace]
[-]poststarthook/start-service-ip-repair-controllers failed: not finished
...
I0115 20:57:06.335471       1 healthz.go:280] informer-sync,poststarthook/start-service-ip-repair-controllers check failed: readyz
[-]informer-sync failed: 1 informers not started yet: [*v1.Secret] # v1.Namespace informer is ready  
[-]poststarthook/start-service-ip-repair-controllers failed: not finished
...
F0115 20:57:18.630248       1 hooks.go:204] PostStartHook "start-service-ip-repair-controllers" failed: unable to perform initial IP and Port allocation check

```

We think this is a race condition introduced by new code path when `MultiCIDRServiceAllocator` is enabled by default in v1.33.  
`start-service-ip-repair-controllers` reads clusterIPs from all `Services` objects and creates `IPAddresses` objects if they are not found from cache. Since we are upgrading from v1.32, where `MultiCIDRServiceAllocator` is disabled, ETCD does not contain any `IPAddresses` objects. 
`start-service-ip-repair-controllers` therefore does not read any existing `IPAddresses` objects from cache and attempts to create them. However, at this point, the `ipaddresses.networking.k8s.io` API is not yet ready. As a result, `start-service-ip-repair-controllers` failes and the kube-apiserver never becomes ready.

Because we have a large number of namespaces, `v1.Namespace` informer takes more time to become ready, which increases the likelihood of this issue occurring in our cluster.
In v1.32 `MultiCIDRServiceAllocator` is disabled. The `start-service-ip-repair-controllers`  implementation only invokes the internal `RangeRegistry` API, which is initialized earlier, so this issue did not exist.



### What did you expect to happen?

The kube-apiserver should start successfully and the repair controller should create missing `IPAddress` objects for existing `Services`, either by:
1. Waiting for admission plugins to be ready before attempting writes
2. Deferring repair work until after startup completes
3. Retrying failed operations instead of terminating

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Prerequisites:
- Cluster with large number of `Namespaces` and `Services` 
- `MultiCIDRServiceAllocator` feature gate previously disabled

Steps:
1. Prepare v1.33 kube-apiserver manifests with `MultiCIDRServiceAllocator` enabled by default
2. Start kube-apiserver
3. Observe API server fails to start

items.body:
### What happened?

When creating a Service with ipFamilyPolicy: RequireDualStack or PreferredDualstack on Windows nodes, kube-proxy sometimes programs incorrect load balancers.

The issue manifests in two main ways:

1. Incorrect backend selection
    - IPv6 endpoints are sometimes programmed as backends for IPv4 VIPs
    - IPv4 endpoints are sometimes programmed as backends for IPv6 VIPs
    - This results in traffic blackholing or connection failures

2. Incorrect load balancer flags
   - IPv6-specific HNS flags are sometimes applied to IPv4 load balancers
   - IPv4 flags are sometimes applied to IPv6 load balancers
   - This causes inconsistent behavior and unexpected failures in datapath programming

These issues appear intermittent and are more frequently observed under:

- Endpoint updates
- Service updates
- Rapid pod churn 

### What did you expect to happen?

For a RequireDualStack Service:

- IPv4 VIPs should:
    - Use only IPv4 endpoints
    - Be programmed with IPv4-specific HNS flags

- IPv6 VIPs should:
    - Use only IPv6 endpoints
    - Be programmed with IPv6-specific HNS flags

The programming behavior should be deterministic and consistent, matching the dual-stack service semantics defined in the Kubernetes dual-stack KEP.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a Windows cluster with:
    - Dual-stack networking enabled
    - Windows nodes using winkernel kube-proxy
2. Create a Service:
 
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: test-dualstack-lb
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  ipFamilyPolicy: RequireDualStack
  ipFamilies:
    - IPv4
    - IPv6
  selector:
    app: test
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 80
```
 
3. Deploy dual-stack pods with both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses
4. Trigger updates:
    - Scale pods up/down
    - Restart kube-proxy
    - Update endpoints or service annotations
5. Observe HNS load balancers and backend programming

### Anything else we need to know?

- This issue appears to be specific to Windows kube-proxy (winkernel).
- This issue violates the dual-stack contract defined in the Kubernetes dual-stack KEP.
